title: The Odyssey
author: Homer
openingText: Tell me, O muse, of that ingenious hero who travelled far and wide after he had sacked the famous town of Troy. Many cities did he visit, and many were the nations with whose manners and customs he was acquainted; moreover he suffered much by sea while trying to save his own life and bring his men safely home; but do what he might he could not save his men, for they perished through their own sheer folly in eating the cattle of the Sun-god Hyperion; so the god prevented them from ever reaching home. Tell me, too, about all these things, O daughter of Jove, from whatsoever source you may know them. So now all who escaped death in battle or by shipwreck had got safely home except Odysseus, and he, though he was longing to return to his wife and country, was detained by the goddess Calypso, who had got him into a large cave and wanted to marry him.
about:
The Odyssey is the ten-year journey of Odysseus home from the Trojan War. He survives sea monsters, witches, the Cyclops, the underworld, and Calypso's island; he arrives home to find his wife besieged by suitors and his son grown. The poem is the homecoming after the war the Iliad described — and the question of whether you can come home at all when you have been gone so long.

Like the Iliad, the Odyssey was composed orally in Greek around the 8th century BCE and attributed to Homer. It is shorter than the Iliad, more episodic, and lighter in tone. It is the founding adventure story in Western literature and has been read as that, but it is also a serious treatment of cunning, marriage, and the duties owed to strangers.

angleCards.title: Comfort vs. the journey.
angleCards.text: Odysseus is offered immortality and refuses it. Why does he? And what does it cost him to keep saying no?
angleCards.angleObjective: I want to understand what Odysseus keeps refusing — and why choosing the hard road home over an easy life still matters.

angleCards.title: Greek ethics vs. Christianity.
angleCards.text: Homer's world runs on honour and consequence, not grace. Odysseus kills every suitor when he returns, and it feels right. Understanding why is one of the sharpest contrasts in Western literature.
angleCards.angleObjective: I want to understand Greek ethics — a moral world without forgiveness — and what it reveals when contrasted with Christianity.

angleCards.title: Fatherhood and absence.
angleCards.text: The poem opens with Telemachus, who has never known his father. His journey runs parallel to Odysseus's throughout — both looking for the same thing.
angleCards.angleObjective: I want to follow the father-son story — Telemachus growing up without his father, and what happens when they finally meet.

angleCards.title: Intelligence over force.
angleCards.text: Odysseus is not the strongest warrior. He is the one who thinks. Homer's quiet argument — that cunning outlasts brute strength — runs through every episode.
angleCards.angleObjective: I want to follow the argument that intelligence beats force — that cunning is the highest virtue — and see how Homer makes that case.

cast.name: Odysseus
cast.description: King of Ithaca. Ten years trying to get home. Survives by thinking, not by force.

cast.name: Penelope
cast.description: Waiting twenty years. Outwitting a hundred men who want to replace her husband.

cast.name: Telemachus
cast.description: Never knew his father. His coming-of-age runs parallel to Odysseus's journey home.

cast.name: Athena
cast.description: Odysseus's champion. She respects him because he thinks. Appears in disguise throughout.

cast.name: Poseidon
cast.description: Hates Odysseus for blinding his son Polyphemus. Most obstacles trace back to him.

cast.name: The Suitors
cast.description: Over a hundred men in Odysseus's palace, eating his food, competing for Penelope.

whyItMatters.title: The Original Adventure
whyItMatters.body: Almost every adventure story since — Sinbad, Robinson Crusoe, Star Wars — is in conversation with the Odyssey. The pattern of leaving home, surviving impossible obstacles, and returning changed is set here.

whyItMatters.title: The Hero of Cunning
whyItMatters.body: Where Achilles is great because of strength, Odysseus is great because of intelligence. He lies, he plans, he disguises himself, he uses words. The poem argues that survival requires a different kind of greatness from war.

whyItMatters.title: Coming Home Is Its Own Trial
whyItMatters.body: The last quarter of the poem is about Odysseus arriving in Ithaca and not yet being able to be himself. He returns disguised as a beggar; he tests his wife and son; he finally has to fight to retake his own house. The poem suggests that homecoming is harder than any of the monsters before it.
